title: A generic Sylow-elimination lemma: order 5·m forces a normal Sylow 5-subgroup
description: The verified Abel–Ruffini proof that x⁵−4x+2 is not solvable by radicals (parent AbelRuffiniOQ04OQ01) rules out |Gal| ∈ {10, 20, 40} with three essentially verbatim private lemmas gal_card_ne_10 / _20 / _40. Each is a Sylow argument on a subgroup G ≤ S₅ of order 5·m (m = 2, 4, 8): the Sylow 5-subgroup has order 5, the count n₅ divides m and is ≡ 1 (mod 5) forcing n₅ = 1, so the Sylow 5-subgroup is normal and equals ⟨c⟩ for any order-5 element c; only the final 'no transposition normalizes a 5-cycle' step is specific to S₅. Open question oq-03 asks to factor the shared skeleton — a pure group-theory fact depending solely on the group order — into a single generic lemma parameterized by the order. This entry does exactly that, fully abstractly (no Polynomial.Gal, no permutations, no native_decide): zpowers_order5_normal proves that in ANY finite group of order 5·m with 5 ∤ m and the only divisor d ∣ m with d ≡ 1 (mod 5) being d = 1, the cyclic subgroup generated by any order-5 element is normal; conj_mem_zpowers_order5 is the immediate corollary that every element normalizes ⟨c⟩. The three original orders 10 = 5·2, 20 = 5·4, 40 = 5·8 are recovered as examples discharging the divisor hypothesis for m ∈ {2, 4, 8}.

originalContributions: zpowers_order5_normal: for any finite group G with Nat.card G = 5·m, 5 ∤ m, and (∀ d ∣ m, d ≡ 1 mod 5 → d = 1), the subgroup ⟨c⟩ generated by any order-5 element c is normal — the shared group-theoretic core of the three verbatim lemmas gal_card_ne_10/_20/_40, lifted to an arbitrary group and parameterized by the order.
conj_mem_zpowers_order5: the corollary that under those hypotheses every g satisfies g·c·g⁻¹ ∈ ⟨c⟩ — the exact 'hconj_zpow' step reused in all three original lemmas.

A native_decide-free proof of the Sylow-order computation (order 5·m has Sylow 5-subgroup of order exactly 5) via Nat.factorization_mul, replacing the concrete native_decide calls of the private lemmas and yielding a 0-axiom result.
Explicit examples verifying the divisor hypothesis for m ∈ {2, 4, 8}, recovering the three original orders 10, 20, 40 from the single generic lemma.

overview.historicalContext: In the classical proof that a specific quintic such as x⁵ − 4x + 2 is not solvable by radicals, one computes its Galois group over ℚ and shows it is the full symmetric group S₅. A key step eliminates the intermediate possibilities |Gal| ∈ {10, 20, 40}. All three are handled by the same Sylow argument: a transitive subgroup of S₅ of order 5·m (m = 2, 4, 8) has a unique — hence normal — Sylow 5-subgroup, generated by a 5-cycle, which no transposition can normalize. In the formalized proof these appeared as three nearly identical private lemmas. Sylow's theorems (1872) are exactly the tool that makes the uniqueness argument uniform across the three orders, since in each case the number of Sylow 5-subgroups n₅ divides the 5′-part m and satisfies n₅ ≡ 1 (mod 5), whose only common solution is n₅ = 1.
overview.problemStatement: Factor the three verbatim Sylow-elimination lemmas gal_card_ne_10 / _20 / _40 — which differ only in the group order 10, 20, 40 — into a single generic lemma parameterized by the order. Isolate the pure group-theoretic content (independent of the symmetric group and of Galois theory): in a finite group of order 5·m with 5 ∤ m and no divisor d of m with d ≡ 1 (mod 5) other than 1, the cyclic subgroup generated by any order-5 element is normal.
overview.proofStrategy: Let G be finite with Nat.card G = 5·m, 5 ∤ m. (1) Order of the Sylow 5-subgroup: Sylow.card_eq_multiplicity gives |P₅| = 5^(v₅(|G|)); since |G| = 5·m and 5 ∤ m, Nat.factorization_mul plus Nat.factorization_eq_zero_of_not_dvd give v₅(5·m) = 1, so |P₅| = 5 (no native_decide needed). (2) Uniqueness: the index of P₅ is m (from index·|P₅| = |G|), and card_sylow_modEq_one together with Sylow.card_dvd_index give n₅ ∣ m and n₅ ≡ 1 (mod 5); the divisor hypothesis huniq forces n₅ = 1. (3) Normality: a unique Sylow subgroup is normal — Subsingleton (Sylow 5 G) and Sylow.smul_eq_iff_mem_normalizer show every element lies in the normalizer. (4) Identification with ⟨c⟩: for an order-5 element c, IsPGroup.exists_le_sylow places ⟨c⟩ inside a Sylow subgroup, which by uniqueness is P₅; a cardinality-matching bijection (both have order 5) gives P₅ = ⟨c⟩. Transporting normality along this equality yields (⟨c⟩).Normal. The corollary conj_mem_zpowers_order5 is then Normal.conj_mem.
keyInsights: The three orders 10, 20, 40 differ only in the 5′-part m ∈ {2, 4, 8}; every other line of the three original lemmas is byte-for-byte identical. The right abstraction is therefore a lemma quantified over the group order 5·m, with the arithmetic that varies (which divisors of m are ≡ 1 mod 5) packaged as a single hypothesis huniq.

Uniqueness of the Sylow 5-subgroup, not its explicit description, is what delivers normality; Sylow's third theorem (n₅ ∣ m and n₅ ≡ 1 mod 5) is exactly the mechanism that turns a statement about the order into n₅ = 1 for all three m simultaneously.

The divisibility hypothesis in huniq is genuinely needed for m = 8: the divisor 6 satisfies 6 ≡ 1 (mod 5), and only 6 ∤ 8 rules it out. The congruence alone does not suffice — this is why huniq takes both d ∣ m and d % 5 = 1.

Abstracting away from S₅ eliminates the concrete native_decide calls used in the private lemmas to compute the Sylow order; the arithmetic v₅(5·m) = 1 is proved symbolically via Nat.factorization_mul, making the generic lemma 0-axiom where the specializations were not.

sections.title: Sylow 5-Subgroup Has Order 5 and Is Unique
sections.summary: The 5-part of |G| = 5·m is exactly 5 (Nat.factorization_mul + factorization_eq_zero_of_not_dvd, no native_decide), so |P₅| = 5. Its index is m, and Sylow's third theorem (card_sylow_modEq_one, Sylow.card_dvd_index) gives n₅ ∣ m with n₅ ≡ 1 (mod 5); huniq forces n₅ = 1.

sections.title: Normality and Identification with ⟨c⟩
sections.summary: Uniqueness gives Subsingleton (Sylow 5 G), hence P₅ is normal via Sylow.smul_eq_iff_mem_normalizer. For an order-5 element c, IsPGroup.exists_le_sylow puts ⟨c⟩ ≤ P₅; a cardinality bijection (both order 5) upgrades this to P₅ = ⟨c⟩, and normality transports to ⟨c⟩.

sections.title: Normalization Corollary and the Three Orders
sections.summary: conj_mem_zpowers_order5: every g normalizes ⟨c⟩ (Normal.conj_mem). Three examples verify the divisor hypothesis for m = 2, 4, 8, recovering the original orders 10 = 5·2, 20 = 5·4, 40 = 5·8; the m = 8 case highlights that 6 ≡ 1 (mod 5) is excluded only because 6 ∤ 8.

conclusion.summary: The three verbatim private lemmas gal_card_ne_10 / _20 / _40 of the Abel–Ruffini x⁵−4x+2 proof are factored into one generic, fully abstract lemma: in any finite group of order 5·m with 5 ∤ m and no divisor d ∣ m with d ≡ 1 (mod 5) except d = 1, the cyclic subgroup generated by any order-5 element is normal (zpowers_order5_normal), and consequently every element normalizes it (conj_mem_zpowers_order5). The orders 10, 20, 40 are the m ∈ {2, 4, 8} instances. Follow-up OQ04·OQ01·OQ03·OQ01 lifts this core from the fixed prime 5 to an arbitrary prime p (zpowers_sylow_normal / conj_mem_zpowers_sylow); the fixed-5 lemma zpowers_order5_normal is now a one-line corollary. Generalizing the prime is not cosmetic: variable p forces Nat.mod_eq_of_lt (to evaluate 1 % p) and Nat.eq_of_mul_eq_mul_right (nonlinear index cancellation [G:P]·p = p·m), steps that omega/interval_cases discharge automatically only for the concrete numeral 5.
conclusion.significance: Replaces three near-duplicate Sylow arguments with a single reusable group-theory lemma parameterized by the group order, isolating the content that is independent of the symmetric group and of Galois theory. The abstraction also removes the native_decide calls of the specializations, so the generic core is 0-axiom verified.
implications: Any order-5-cycle normality argument in a group of order 5·m (with the divisor condition) now reduces to a single lemma application, as the three original orders demonstrate.

Provides exactly the 'g normalizes ⟨c⟩' input that the S₅-specific 'no transposition normalizes a 5-cycle' step consumes, cleanly separating the group-order arithmetic from the permutation-theoretic contradiction.
openQuestions: Generalize from the prime 5 to an arbitrary prime p: in a group of order p·m with p ∤ m and the analogous divisor hypothesis, the subgroup generated by any order-p element is normal.

Replace the divisor hypothesis huniq by the sharper structural condition on m under which a group of order p·m must have a normal Sylow p-subgroup, and characterize exactly which orders 5·m force normality.
